import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def make_orders():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
    n = 240
    category = rng.choice(["Home", "Electronics", "Beauty", "Sports"], size=n, p=[0.35, 0.2, 0.25, 0.2])

        "shipping_days": rng.integers(1, 9, n),

    df["revenue"] = (df["quantity"] * df["unit_price"]).round(2)
    return df.sort_values("order_date").reset_index(drop=True)

orders = make_orders()
orders["month"] = orders["order_date"].dt.month
table = orders.pivot_table(index="month", columns="category", values="revenue", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0).round(0)

guided.title: Choose the export
guided.prompt: A colleague must send an interactive revenue chart to a client by email, and also add a static copy to a PDF report. Say which export you use for each, what the HTML option `include_plotlyjs` changes, and one risk of sending the HTML.
guided.solution: For the email, use `fig.write_html("revenue.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn")`: the client opens the page in a browser and keeps hover and zoom. With `include_plotlyjs="cdn"` the file is small because the Plotly library is loaded from the internet when the page opens (so it needs a connection); the default embeds the library and makes the file several megabytes but self-contained. For the PDF use a static image from `fig.write_image(...)`, which needs the Kaleido package installed, or a screenshot, because a PDF cannot run the JavaScript. The risk of the HTML is that it carries all the data behind the chart, which the client can read from the page source, so aggregate or remove sensitive rows first.
hints: Where will each chart be read?
rubric: HTML for the email, static image for the PDF.
Names that the HTML contains the underlying data.

independent.title: Design a three-panel dashboard
independent.prompt: Design (in code and one paragraph) a figure with three panels: a line of monthly total revenue, a bar of revenue by category and a histogram of order revenue, with `make_subplots`, one finding-style title, a hover that shows revenue with a thousands separator and an HTML export. Explain how you keep it readable.
independent.starter:
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

# fig = make_subplots(...)
independent.solution:
```python
fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=3, subplot_titles=("Revenue by month", "Revenue by category", "Order sizes"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=list(monthly.index), y=list(monthly.values), name="Month"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=list(by_cat.index), y=list(by_cat.values), name="Category"), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Histogram(x=orders["revenue"], nbinsx=12, name="Orders"), row=1, col=3)
fig.update_traces(hovertemplate="%{y:,.0f}<extra>%{fullData.name}</extra>", selector=dict(type="scatter"))
fig.update_layout(title="Revenue is steady by month and concentrated in Electronics", showlegend=False)
fig.write_html("dashboard.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn")
```

It stays readable by giving each panel one question and its own subplot title, turning off the legend because panel titles name the series, keeping the same colour for the same thing and putting the finding in the figure title. A hover is added for exact numbers but nothing depends on it. The hover template is applied to the scatter trace only because the bar and histogram use different hover fields.
rubric: Uses make_subplots with three panels and subplot titles.
Adds a Scatter, a Bar and a Histogram with row/col.
Finding-style title; hover format with thousands separator.
Exports with write_html and explains readability choices.

environment.note: Examples 2 to 5 use plotly, which the browser cannot load: run them on your own computer after `pip install plotly pandas numpy`. They print figure properties instead of showing the chart; open an exported HTML file in a browser to see the interactivity. Static image export (`write_image`) needs the extra Kaleido package and is not run here. Example 1 and the graded exercises are pandas only and run in the browser. Written exercises are self-assessed.

checks.question: What does `fig.update_layout(hovermode='x unified')` do?
options: Shows one hover box listing every series at the pointer's x position
checks.explanation: Unified hover compares all series at the same x, ideal for time series. It does not merge traces.

checks.question: A figure has 4 traces and a button has `args=[{'visible': [True, False]}]`. What goes wrong?
options: The list length does not match the number of traces
The button is ignored silently and the chart is blank
checks.explanation: The visible list needs one entry per trace in order. A short list gives unexpected visibility; build it from the trace names.

checks.question: What is `fig.to_json()` for?
options: Storing or sending the figure as a data and layout string
checks.explanation: It serialises the figure to JSON with the keys data and layout. Images and HTML are other exports.

checks.question: Why does `write_html(..., include_plotlyjs='cdn')` produce a smaller file?
options: The library is linked from the internet instead of embedded
checks.explanation: The default embeds the Plotly library in the page. With cdn the page loads it when opened, so it needs a connection.

checks.question: A dropdown button changes the visible series. Where does the data for the hidden series live?
options: Inside the figure; all traces are stored and only shown or hidden
On a server queried by the button
checks.explanation: Buttons with method update only change properties of traces that already exist, so all the data travels with the figure.
